paras: The lynching of George Martin was the killing of a miner by a mob near Warrior, Jefferson County, Alabama, on the night of May 1, 1888, hours after he was accused of shooting the town's acting marshal, Owen Kelly. Officers tried to move Martin to Birmingham in the caboose of a freight train, but a mob stopped the train, took him from his guards, hanged him to a tree and shot his body. The story ran nationally as a wire item, sometimes naming him Morton.

Late on the afternoon of May 1, that paper's first dispatch said, Martin was drunk and "raised a row" in front of a saloon, and when Kelly tried to arrest him, Martin shot him dead. A Warrior correspondent of the Huntsville Gazette wrote that George and Will Martin were "drunk and disorderly" when Kelly interfered "in behalf of law and order."

Kelly had held the post for less than twenty-four hours. He was filling in for his kinsman, Marshal John Kelley, who had gone to Knoxville after William Dodd, said to have killed a man at Warrior two weeks before and to have "barely escaped a mob."

Martin ran, firing at the crowd that chased him; the first dispatch said he hit no one and was caught on the edge of town, while the Huntsville letter said both brothers fled into the country before they were captured. He was locked up with his brother William, who was arrested for the same brawl.

Fearing a lynching, the mayor telegraphed Sheriff Truss in Birmingham, who prepared to send men and rifles on the midnight train. Before the sheriff left, Warrior officers put Martin aboard the caboose of a freight train bound for Birmingham, hoping to get ahead of the "would-be lynchers."

The mob learned of the plan, seized the train, and uncoupled the caboose, with Martin, his brother and four guards inside. According to the Appeal, Martin told the mob from the car door that he alone had done the killing, asked the guards for a gun and was refused, and then walked out into the crowd, asking that his brother be spared. He was hanged to a tree, and about half a dozen men emptied their guns and pistols into his body. The Huntsville correspondent put the mob at "several hundred men" and wrote that the body was left hanging.

The train reached Birmingham at 2:30 a.m. with the news, and William Martin, "bespattered with his brother's blood," was jailed there. A Charlotte paper noted that the sheriff "failed to go." No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members, or of a trial appears in the coverage.

The Memphis Appeal carried two special dispatches from Birmingham, the first headed "Killed a Marshal" with "Fears of Lynching" and the second "A Nervy Man." The New York Evening World condensed that account under "The Mob StrungHim Up," and Missouri's Butler Weekly Times reprinted it in full as "Murdered by a Mob," with the subhead "The Man Cool."

A shorter wire ran in Savannah under "Murdar and Lynching" and in Maysville, Kentucky, as "Another Alabama Lynching"; some copies named the man Morton, and the Omaha Daily Bee placed the event at "Warren." Into mid-May the item appeared in news-summary columns in Minnesota, Mississippi, Arkansas and North Carolina. The Forrest City Times in Arkansas added that it was "the third lynching in that county within a month."

The only account from Warrior itself, the Huntsville Gazette letter headed "Murder and Jude [Judge] Lynch Busy," called Kelly's death "another terrible crime" and closed by treating the affair as "another temperance lecture" against whiskey. Neither it nor the wire reports passed judgment on the mob, named any of its members, or stated the race of Martin or Kelly.

The fuller Birmingham dispatches and the Warrior letter name the victim George Martin, while one version of the short wire, carried in Maysville and Oxford, Mississippi, gives George Morton. The Birmingham dispatches, dated May 1 and 2, put the lynching on the night after the shooting, before the train reached the city at 2:30 a.m.; the Forrest City Times instead dated the shooting to a Thursday and the hanging to 11 o'clock.

reader.title: Lynching of George Martin
bases: A mob seized a prisoner accused of killing a town marshal from officers on a freight train, hanged him and shot his body (A2, A4, A12).

Martin was taken from four guards by a mob (several hundred men in the local letter), hanged and shot, as punishment for the killing of the marshal (A4, A12); no lawful authority is claimed in any report (A2, A5).

The Memphis Appeal's Birmingham dispatches, a separate short wire, and a Warrior correspondent's letter to the Huntsville Gazette agree on the shooting, the seizure from officers, the hanging and the shooting of the body (A2, A4, A12).

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal headed its second dispatch 'A Nervy Man,' calling the lynchers 'Vigilantes' and a 'Howling Mob' while stressing Martin's coolness.
The first Appeal dispatch led with the marshal's killing ('Killed a Marshal') and 'Fears of Lynching.'
Short wire versions ran under 'Murdar and Lynching' and 'Another Alabama Lynching' and in news-summary columns.
The Butler Weekly Times reprint was headed 'Murdered by a Mob,' with the subhead 'An Alabama Marshal Killer Hanged and Then Shot-The Man Cool.'
The Huntsville Gazette letter called Kelly's killing 'another terrible crime' and drew a temperance lesson, saying nothing for or against the mob.
